questions.q: Why does the `build_ghz_circuit` docstring explicitly state 'Not yet validated against real hardware' rather than omitting that line?
options: Because stating gaps is required by Qiskit's license
Because Lesson 4 argued documentation should state what's actually been checked, and omitting this would overstate validation coverage that doesn't yet exist
Because real hardware validation is impossible in principle
Because the line is irrelevant filler with no real purpose
questions.explain: Lesson 4's documentation standard specifically calls for an honest 'Validated against' field. Omitting the real-hardware caveat would silently imply broader validation than the library has actually received.

questions.q: What does the README's 'Validated against' section include that goes beyond simple installation instructions?
options: Only a pip install command
Which specific backends (e.g. LocalSimulatorBackend) the full test suite has actually been validated against, and an honest statement that real hardware is not yet validated
A list of unrelated marketing claims
The personal contact information of the library's author
questions.explain: The README documents concretely which backends have actually been validated (simulator) and which haven't (real hardware), giving a user accurate information about what to trust, consistent with Lesson 4's documentation standard.

questions.q: Why does the example script print the z-score and the specific confidence threshold (2.58, 99%) rather than just printing 'PASS' or 'FAIL'?
options: Because Python cannot print booleans
So a new user learns not just the verdict but the standard it was judged against, consistent with every statistical test's documented confidence level built across Chapter 2
Because z-scores are required output for all print statements
Because PASS/FAIL alone would cause a syntax error
questions.explain: Printing the explicit z-score and confidence threshold used continues the lesson's running theme (from Chapters 2 and 4) that a statistical verdict is only meaningful alongside the specific confidence level it was judged against.

questions.q: What is the purpose of `docs/reproducibility.md` in the capstone's documentation, according to the lesson?
options: To list the library's dependencies only
To model Lesson 17's reproducibility practices (tagging, lockfile, experiment records, fire-drill reproduction) as a template for users extending the library with their own experiments
To replace the need for a README entirely
To document unrelated marketing copy
questions.explain: docs/reproducibility.md walks through the same tag/lockfile/experiment-record/fire-drill steps from Lesson 17, giving future users of the library a concrete template to follow for their own reproducible experiments rather than reinventing the practice.

questions.q: Based on the README's stated gap (no real-hardware validation yet) and Chapter 4's practices, what would a user need to add to report a trustworthy, reproducible result from running the Grover module on real hardware?
options: Nothing -- the library's existing documentation and tests are already sufficient for any backend
A git tag for their experiment, a committed lockfile for their environment, and an experiment record capturing shots, seeds where applicable, backend name, and a calibration timestamp (Lessons 14-16)
Only a screenshot of the output
A completely new, separate library written from scratch
questions.explain: Since the library itself hasn't been validated on hardware, a user running it there would need to apply Chapter 4's full reproducibility practice themselves -- tagging the commit, locking their environment, and recording run parameters including a calibration timestamp (Lesson 16) in place of a simulator seed -- to produce a trustworthy, reproducible claim.
